query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: For AlCrFeNiSi additive-manufactured miniature components, implementing an in-situ, machine-learning‐optimized pulsed laser energy regime (with a transient remelting step and substrate pre-heating) will reduce thermal gradients, promote a refined and stress‐relieved microstructure, and thereby overcome residual stress issues and mechanical degradation seen in conventional high‐thermal-load processes.
generation.material_initial_state: Spherical, gas-atomized AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock prepared for LPBF processing.
generation.intervention: Adopt a pulsed laser power deposition strategy guided by machine learning optimization that incorporates an in-situ remelting step and substrate pre-heating (e.g., to ~200°C) to moderate the thermal input during build.
generation.conditions: Process miniature components (approximately 5 mm cubes) using an energy density window reduced by about 20–30% relative to standard continuous high-power LPBF, with an optimized scan speed and laser pulsing schedule; test under standard room-temperature and elevated-temperature mechanical testing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined grain structure with lower dislocation density and minimized phase segregation, achieved by reducing extreme thermal gradients during solidification.
generation.mechanism: The pulsed energy regime lowers instantaneous thermal input, enabling periodic in-situ remelting that relieves thermal stresses and permits uniform grain nucleation; substrate pre-heating further decreases thermal shock, leading to a more homogeneous microstructure with enhanced mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional high-power processing, components produced with the intervention are expected to show reduced residual stresses, higher yield strength and ductility, and simplified defect control.
generation.baseline: Components produced using standard continuous high-power LPBF, which typically suffer from significant thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity.
generation.boundary: This intervention’s efficacy is anticipated for the small-scale (e.g., 5 mm) geometry of miniature components and may be less effective in drastically larger geometries or for alloys with markedly different thermal characteristics.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in mechanical properties and stress reduction remains to be empirically determined, and the scalability of the method to more complex geometries needs further validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two groups of identical miniature components using AlCrFeNiSi powder: one group by conventional continuous high-power LPBF and the other by the machine-learning-guided pulsed regime with in-situ remelting and substrate pre-heating. Analyze each group for residual stress (via X-ray diffraction), grain structure and defect density (via SEM/TEM), and mechanical performance (via tensile and compression tests).
measurements: Residual stress profiles measured by X-ray diffraction
Grain size and dislocation density via electron microscopy
Mechanical properties such as yield strength, ductility, and hardness through standardized tests
Density and porosity using micro-computed tomography
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pulsed regime samples do not show statistically significant reductions in residual stress and improvements in mechanical properties or microstructural homogeneity compared to the conventional process, the hypothesis will be falsified.

Material-agnostic machine learning approach enables high relative density in powder bed fusion products

Abstract: This study introduces a method that is applicable across various powder materials to predict process conditions that yield a product with a relative density greater than 98% by laser powder bed fusion. We develop an XGBoost model using a dataset comprising material properties of powder and process conditions, and its output, relative density, undergoes a transformation using a sigmoid function to increase accuracy. We deeply examine the relationships between input features and the target value using Shapley additive explanations. Experimental validation with stainless steel 316 L, AlSi10Mg, and Fe60Co15Ni15Cr10 medium entropy alloy powders verifies the method’s reproducibility and transferability. This research contributes to laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing by offering a universally applicable strategy to optimize process conditions. Additive manufacturing of alloys with programmable microstructure and properties

Abstract: AbstractIn metallurgy, mechanical deformation is essential to engineer the microstructure of metals and to tailor their mechanical properties. However, this practice is inapplicable to near-net-shape metal parts produced by additive manufacturing (AM), since it would irremediably compromise their carefully designed geometries. In this work, we show how to circumvent this limitation by controlling the dislocation density and thermal stability of a steel alloy produced by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) technology. We show that by manipulating the alloy’s solidification structure, we can ‘program’ recrystallization upon heat treatment without using mechanical deformation. When employed site-specifically, our strategy enables designing and creating complex microstructure architectures that combine recrystallized and non-recrystallized regions with different microstructural features and properties. We show how this heterogeneity may be conducive to materials with superior performance compared to those with monolithic microstructure. Additive manufacturing of an ultrastrong, deformable Al alloy with nanoscale intermetallics

Abstract: AbstractLight-weight, high-strength, aluminum (Al) alloys have widespread industrial applications. However, most commercially available high-strength Al alloys, like AA 7075, are not suitable for additive manufacturing due to their high susceptibility to solidification cracking. In this work, a custom Al alloy Al92Ti2Fe2Co2Ni2 is fabricated by selective laser melting. Heterogeneous nanoscale medium-entropy intermetallic lamella form in the as-printed Al alloy. Macroscale compression tests reveal a combination of high strength, over 700 MPa, and prominent plastic deformability. Micropillar compression tests display significant back stress in all regions, and certain regions have flow stresses exceeding 900 MPa. Post-deformation analyses reveal that, in addition to abundant dislocation activities in Al matrix, complex dislocation structures and stacking faults form in monoclinic Al9Co2 type brittle intermetallics.
